questions.question_text: Mild, nonpsychotic depression with predominant anxiety is called

correct_answer.text: Dysthymia

correct_answers.text: Dysthymia

questions.explanation: Dysthymia is defined as a reactive nonpsychotic depression of mild to moderate intensity with predominant anxiety[cite: 7]. It is characterized by the presence of a depressed mood that lasts most of the day and is present almost continuously[cite: 7]. Patients complain that they have always been depressed[cite: 7]. It is not a sequela to a major depressive episode as with chronic depression[cite: 7]. There are associated feelings of inadequacy, guilt, irritability, and anger; withdrawal from society; loss of interest; and inactivity and lack of productivity[cite: 7]. Most cases are of early onset, beginning in childhood or adolescence and certainly by the time patients reach their 20s[cite: 7]. The overall prognosis for dysthymia is good with treatment; however, 25 percent of dysthymic patients never attain complete recovery[cite: 7]. Bipolar disorder is defined as a mood disorder in which the patient exhibits both manic and depressive episodes[cite: 7]. The criteria for a manic episode require the presence of a distinct period of abnormal mood lasting at least 1 week[cite: 7]. Typically beginning in the teenage years, the 20s, or the 30s, the first episode of bipolar I disorder could be manic, depressive, or mixed[cite: 7]. On average, manic episodes predominate in youth, and depressive episodes predominate in later years[cite: 7]. Although the overall sex ratio is 1:1, men, on average, undergo more manic episodes, and women experience more mixed and depressive episodes[cite: 7]. Endogenomorphic depression is a term used to describe inhibition of the pleasure or reward system to such an extent that the patient no longer has the capacity for enjoyment[cite: 7]. There may or may not be an apparent environmental precipitant or stress[cite: 7]. In most cases, patients show dramatic abnormalities in psychomotor activity and somatic rhythms (i.e., sleep, appetite, libido)[cite: 7]. Such patients may also be delusional[cite: 7]. The symptom profile in chronic depression usually displays low-grade intensity[cite: 7]. Full criteria for a major depressive episode must have been met continuously for at least the past 2 years[cite: 7]. Instead of the customary remission within 1 year, patients are ill for years[cite: 7]. Anxiety disorders are disorders in which anxiety is the most prominent disturbance or in which patients experience anxiety if they resist giving in to their symptoms[cite: 7]. They are among the most prevalent mental disorders in the general population[cite: 7]. Women are affected nearly twice as frequently as men[cite: 7]. They are associated with significant morbidity and often are chronic and resistant to treatment[cite: 7]. They include (1) panic disorder with or without agoraphobia, (2) agoraphobia with or without panic disorder, (3) specific phobia, (4) social phobia, (5) obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), (6) posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), (7) acute stress disorder, and (8) generalized anxiety disorder[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: The most consistent computer tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abnormality observed in depressive disorders is

options.text: increased frequency of hyperintensities in subcortical regions

correct_answer.text: increased frequency of hyperintensities in subcortical regions

correct_answers.text: increased frequency of hyperintensities in subcortical regions

questions.explanation: Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans provide sensitive, noninvasive methods to assess the brain, including cortical and subcortical tracts, as well as white matter lesions[cite: 7]. The most consistent abnormality observed in the depressive disorders is increased frequency of abnormal hyperintensities in subcortical regions, especially the periventricular area, basal ganglia, and thalamus (Figure 15.2)[cite: 7]. More common in bipolar I disorder and among the elderly, these hyperintensities appear to reflect the deleterious neurodegenerative effects of recurrent mood episodes[cite: 7]. Ventricular enlargement, cortical atrophy, and sulcal widening have also been reported in patients with mood disorders compared with normal control subjects[cite: 7]. In addition to age and illness duration, structural abnormalities are associated with increased illness severity, bipolar status, and increased cortisol levels[cite: 7]. Some depressed patients also may have reduced caudate nucleus volumes, suggesting a defect in the mesocorticolimbic system[cite: 7]. Cerebrovascular factors often involve subcortical frontal and basal ganglia structures and appear particularly relevant to late-life depression[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: The following situations call for a break in doctor–patient confidentiality except

options.text: A patient with a delusional disorder thinks his boss is out to get him and threatens to kill her.
A patient with major depressive disorder who is sexually promiscuous contracts syphilis.
A patient with bipolar I disorder admits he is homosexual.
A patient with conduct disorder thrives on the sexual abuse of young children.
A patient with schizoaffective disorder hallucinates that he can fly.

correct_answer.text: A patient with bipolar I disorder admits he is homosexual.

correct_answers.text: A patient with bipolar I disorder admits he is homosexual.

questions.explanation: Confidentiality refers to the therapist’s responsibility to not release information learned in the course of treatment to third parties[cite: 7]. Confidentiality is an essential ingredient of psychiatric care because it is a prerequisite for patients to be willing to speak freely to therapists[cite: 7]. People would be less likely to go for help and would tend to withhold crucial information if confidentiality was not assured[cite: 7]. There is no reason to break doctor–patient confidentiality in situations involving a patient’s sexual preference (e.g., homosexuality) unless there is some threat to the patient’s safety[cite: 7]. Confidentiality must give way to the responsibility to protect others when a patient makes a credible threat to harm someone (e.g, a patient threatening to kill his boss) or acts in a way that could harm him- or herself (e.g., a patient who thinks he can fly)[cite: 7]. Reportable diseases (e.g.,syphilis) must also be reported to the proper authorities despite the bond of patient confidentiality[cite: 7]. Any suspicion of child abuse must also be reported to the authorities[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: A 27-year-old patient has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder. Before starting this patient on lithium for mood stabilization, which of the following laboratory tests should be obtained?

options.text: Thyroid function tests, creatinine, pregnancy test
Thyroid function tests, creatinine, liver function tests
Thyroid function tests, creatinine, complete blood count
Thyroid function tests, liver function tests, pregnancy test
Thyroid function tests, complete blood count, pregnancy test

correct_answer.text: Thyroid function tests, creatinine, pregnancy test

correct_answers.text: Thyroid function tests, creatinine, pregnancy test

questions.explanation: Lithium (Eskalith), used for mood stabilization in patients with bipolar disorder, is known for its low margin of safety, making frequent monitoring necessary[cite: 7]. Common side effects include gastrointestinal disturbances, nephrotoxicity, hypothyroidism, tremors, leukocytosis, acne, psoriasis flares, hair loss, and edema[cite: 7]. Because of these effects, it is important to get thyroid function tests and renal function tests (creatinine) before starting any patient on this medication[cite: 7]. Lithium is also teratogenic and has been associated with cardiac defects, so a pregnancy test is necessary before lithium therapy[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding mood disorders is false?

options.text: One of four patients with an acute depressive episode will have recurrences throughout life.
Approximately 15 percent of depressed patients eventually commit suicide.
Incidence of depression in younger age groups is increasing.
Manic forms of mood disorders predominate in men.
Depressive disorders are more common in women.

correct_answer.text: One of four patients with an acute depressive episode will have recurrences throughout life.

correct_answers.text: One of four patients with an acute depressive episode will have recurrences throughout life.

questions.explanation: Three (not one) out of four patients with acute depression will experience recurrences, with varying degrees of residual symptoms between episodes[cite: 7]. Of note, although depressive disorders are more common in women, more men than women die of suicide because of more lethal methods chosen[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: All of the following are vegetative disturbances of depression except

correct_answer.text: Hypersexuality

correct_answers.text: Hypersexuality

questions.explanation: Hypersexuality is cardinal sign of mania and usually indicates a mixed episode of bipolar disorder in depressed patients[cite: 7]. The small subgroup of depressed persons with increased sexual drive usually exhibit other atypical features; hence, increased sexual drive is considered the fifth reverse vegetative sign (after even worsening mood, initial insomnia, hypersomnia, and weight gain)[cite: 7]. The biological concomitants of melancholia include profound reductions in appetite (i.e., anorexia or weight loss), sleep (i.e., insomnia), and sexual functioning, as well as alterations in other circadian rhythms, especially worsening of mood and psychomotor performance[cite: 7]. An equally prominent subgroup of depressed persons exhibits a reversal of the vegetative and circadian functions, with increases in appetite and sleep—and sometimes in sexual functioning—and an evening worsening of mood; in this atypical pattern, patients characteristically exhibit mood reactivity and sensitivity to rejection[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Serotonin

options.text: is an important regulator of sleep, appetite, and libido
stores are increased by transient stress and depleted by chronic stress
permits or facilitates goal-directed motor and consummatory behavior in conjunction with norepinephrine and dopamine

correct_answer.text: all of the above

correct_answers.text: all of the above

questions.explanation: Serotoninergic neurons project from the brainstem dorsal raphe nuclei to the cerebral cortex, hypothalamus, thalamus, basal ganglia, septum, and hippocampus[cite: 7]. Serotonin (5-HT) pathways have both inhibitory and facilitatory functions in the brain[cite: 7]. For example, much evidence suggests that 5-HT is an important regulator of sleep, appetite, and libido[cite: 7]. Serotonergic neurons projecting to the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus help to regulate circadian rhythms (e.g., sleep–wake cycles, body temperature, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical axis function)[cite: 7]. Serotonin also permits or facilitates goal-directed motor and consummatory behaviors in conjunction with norepinephrine and dopamine[cite: 7]. Moreover, serotonin inhibits aggressive behavior across mammalian and reptilian species[cite: 7]. There is some evidence that serotonin neurotransmission is partly under genetic control[cite: 7]. Nevertheless, whereas acute stress increases serotonin release transiently, chronic stress eventually depletes serotonin stores[cite: 7]. Chronic stress may also increase synthesis of 5-HT1A autoreceptors in the dorsal raphe nucleus, which further decrease serotonin transmission[cite: 7]. Elevated glucocorticoid levels tend to enhance serotonergic functioning and thus may have significant compensatory effects on chronic stress[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Which graph in Figure 15.1 depicts the pattern with the best future prognosis?

correct_answer.text: A

correct_answers.text: A

questions.explanation: The course of major depressive disorder, recurrent, with no antecedent dysthymic disorder and a period of full remission between the episodes predicts the best future prognosis[cite: 7]. This is depicted in graph A[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Which of the graphs in Figure 15.1 depicts the prototypical course of double depression?

correct_answer.text: D

correct_answers.text: D

questions.explanation: Graph D depicts double depression, which is characterized by recurrent major depressive disorder and antecedent dysthymic disorder with no period of full remission in between the two most recent episodes[cite: 7]. Graph A is the course of major depressive disorder, recurrent, with no antecedent dysthymic disorder and full remission between episodes[cite: 7]. Graph B is the course of major depressive disorder, recurrent, with no antecedent dysthymic disorder but with prominent symptoms persisting between episodes (partial remission is attained)[cite: 7]. Graph C is the rare pattern major depressive disorder, recurrent, with antecedent dysthymic disorder but with full interepisodic recovery[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Double depression is characterized by

options.text: two family members with major depressive disorder concurrently
recurrent major depressive disorder with current symptoms twice as disabling as usual
two episodes of major depressive disorder per month consistently
superimposed bipolar II disorder and atypical depression
recurrent major depressive disorder superimposed with dysthymic disorder

correct_answer.text: recurrent major depressive disorder superimposed with dysthymic disorder

correct_answers.text: recurrent major depressive disorder superimposed with dysthymic disorder

questions.explanation: Double depression is characterized by recurrent major depressive disorder with antecedent dysthymic disorder and no period of full remission between the two most recent episodes[cite: 7]. This pattern is seen in approximately 20 to 25 percent of the persons with major depressive disorder[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Depression and mania share which of the following symptoms?

correct_answer.text: Anger

correct_answers.text: Anger

questions.explanation: Despite their contrasts, depression and mania share such symptoms as irritability, anger, insomnia, and agitation[cite: 7]. Mania is defined as a mood disorder characterized by elation, agitation, hyperactivity, and hyperexcitability[cite: 7]. The clinical features of mania are generally the opposite of those of depression[cite: 7]. Depression is defined as a mental state characterized by feelings of sadness, loneliness, despair, low self-esteem, and self-reproach[cite: 7]. Depression is commonly associated with cases of lowered mood, thinking, self-esteem, and activity[cite: 7]. Mania, on the other hand, is commonly associated with elevated mood, a rush of ideas, psychomotor acceleration, and grandiosity[cite: 7]. An excess of the shared symptoms of escalating intensity suggests a mixed phase of mixed episode of mania and depression occurring simultaneously, commonly called bipolar I disorder[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: The person least likely to develop major depressive disorder in his or her lifetime is

options.text: a 19-year-old woman who was raped 3 weeks ago
a 12-year-old girl mourning the death of her mother
an identical twin of a patient with major depressive disorder who committed suicide

correct_answer.text: a 19-year-old woman who was raped 3 weeks ago

correct_answers.text: a 19-year-old woman who was raped 3 weeks ago

questions.explanation: The 19-year-old rape victim is more likely to develop a variation of posttraumatic stress disorder, which is highest among victims of rape, military combat veterans, and survivors of torture[cite: 7]. Childhood onset of dysthymia similarly presages extremely high rates of depression and bipolar disorder in adulthood[cite: 7]. Monozygotic twins have been shown to have a two- to fourfold increase in concordance rates for mood disorders over dizygotic twins, compelling data for the role of genetic factors in mood disorders[cite: 7]. Parental loss before adolescence is also a well-documented risk factor for adult-onset depression[cite: 7]. Medical problems of many types, such as cancer of the pancreas, multiple sclerosis, and space-occupying lesions of the brain, can produce depression[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: A hypomanic episode differs from a manic episode in that a hypomanic episode

correct_answer.text: lacks psychotic features

correct_answers.text: lacks psychotic features

questions.explanation: A hypomanic episode lacks psychotic features, which can sometimes be associated with mania[cite: 7]. A manic episode is a distinct period of an abnormally and persistent elevated, expansive, or irritable mood lasting for at least 1 week or less if a patient must be hospitalized[cite: 7]. A hypomanic episode lasts at least 4 days and is similar to a manic episode except that it is not sufficiently severe to cause impairment in social or occupational functioning[cite: 7]. Patients often believe that they benefit from the energy and confidence of hypomania[cite: 7]. Diagnostically, history of hypomania is preferably obtained from significant others who have observed the patient; the experience is often pleasant, and the subject may be unaware of it or may tend to deny it[cite: 7]. Both mania and hypomania are associated with inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, distractibility, great physical and mental activity, and overinvolvement in pleasurable behavior[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: The defense mechanism most commonly used in depression is

correct_answer.text: introjection

correct_answers.text: introjection

questions.explanation: In Sigmund Freud’s structural theory, introjection of the lost object into the ego leads to the typical depressive symptoms of a lack of energy available to the ego[cite: 7]. The superego, which is unable to retaliate against the lost object externally, flails out at the psychic representation of the lost object, now internalized in the ego as an introject[cite: 7]. When the ego overcomes or merges with the superego, energy previously bound in the depressive symptoms is released, and mania supervenes with the typical symptoms of excess[cite: 7]. Projection is the unconscious defense mechanism in which a person attributes to another person those generally unconscious ideas, thoughts, feelings, and impulses that are personally undesirable or unacceptable[cite: 7]. Sublimation is an unconscious defense mechanism in which the energy associated with unacceptable impulses or drives is diverted into personally and socially acceptable channels[cite: 7]. Undoing is an unconscious defense mechanism by which a person symbolically acts out to reverse something unacceptable that has already been done or against which the ego must defend itself[cite: 7]. Altruism is regard for and dedication to the welfare of others[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not part of the text revision of the fourth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV-TR) criteria for diagnosing atypical depression?

correct_answer.text: Shortening of REM latency

correct_answers.text: Shortening of REM latency

questions.explanation: Nearly two-thirds of patients with depressive disorders, whether experiencing typical or atypical symptoms, exhibit marked shortening of rapid eye movement (REM) latency, the period from sleep onset to the first REM period[cite: 7]. This fact is not specific to atypical depression as are the other choices listed[cite: 7]. Mood reactivity is characterized by mood elevation in response to something good happening[cite: 7]. Leaden paralysis (a heavy, leaden feelings in one’s arms and legs), hypersomnia, increased appetite, and significant weight gain are also among the features of atypical depression[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: l-Tryptophan

options.text: has been used as an adjuvant to both antidepressants and lithium
has not been associated with any serious side effects
is the amino acid precursor to dopamine
has been used as a stimulant

correct_answer.text: has been used as an adjuvant to both antidepressants and lithium

correct_answers.text: has been used as an adjuvant to both antidepressants and lithium

questions.explanation: l-Tryptophan, the amino acid precursor to serotonin, has been used as an adjuvant to both antidepressants and lithium in the treatment of bipolar I disorder[cite: 7]. Tyrosine is the amino acid precursor to dopamine[cite: 7]. l-Tryptophan has also been used alone as a hypnotic and an antidepressant[cite: 7]. l-Tryptophan and l-tryptophan–containing products have been recalled in the United States because l-tryptophan has been associated with eosinophilia–myalgia syndrome[cite: 7]. The symptoms include fatigue, myalgia, shortness of breath, rashes, and swelling of the extremities[cite: 7]. Congestive heart failure and death can also occur[cite: 7]. Although several studies have shown that l-tryptophan is an efficacious adjuvant in the treatment of mood disorders, it should not be used for any purpose until the problem with eosinophilia–myalgia syndrome is resolved[cite: 7]. Current evidence points to a contaminant in the manufacturing process[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not an indicator of a good prognosis for major depressive disorder?

options.text: No more than one previous hospitalization
A history of more than one previous depressive episode

correct_answer.text: A history of more than one previous depressive episode

correct_answers.text: A history of more than one previous depressive episode

questions.explanation: A history of more than one previous depressive episode is not an indicator of a good prognosis for major depressive disorder[cite: 7]. Rather, it increases the possibility for a poor prognosis[cite: 7]. Other indicators of a poor prognosis include coexisting dysthymic disorder, abuse of alcohol and other substances, and anxiety disorder symptoms[cite: 7]. Men are more likely than women to experience a chronically impaired course[cite: 7]. Mild episodes, the absence of psychotic symptoms, and a short hospital stay are good prognostic indicators[cite: 7]. Psychosocial indicators of a good course include a history of solid friendships during adolescence, stable family functioning, and generally sound social functioning for the 5 years preceding the illness[cite: 7]. Additional good prognostic signs are the absence of a comorbid psychiatric disorder and of a personality disorder, no more than one previous hospitalization for major depressive disorder, and an advanced age of onset[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Reactive depression can best be compared to

correct_answer.text: Adjustment disorder

correct_answers.text: Adjustment disorder

questions.explanation: Reactive depression is defined as depression that results from a specific life event[cite: 7]. It continues as long as the event is present, and it terminates with the reversal of the event (e.g., return of a lover after a breakup)[cite: 7]. With interpersonal support, most people can face life’s reversals, which explains why reactive depression tends to be self-limiting[cite: 7]. Hence, adjustment disorder is the more appropriate diagnosis for many cases of reactive depression[cite: 7]. Oppositional defiant disorderis a recurring pattern of negative, hostile, disobedient, and defiant behavior in a child or adolescent, lasting for at least 6 months without serious violation of the basic rights of others[cite: 7]. Conduct disorderis a childhood behavioral condition involving a pattern of repetitive and persistent conduct that infringes on the basic rights of others or does not conform to established societal norms or rules that are appropriate for a child of that age[cite: 7]. Atypical depression is characterized by “reversed vegetative symptoms,” which include oversleeping, overeating, rejection sensitivity, and temporary brightening of mood in response to positive events[cite: 7]. Schizoaffective disorder is a disorder with symptoms of both schizophrenia and manic-depressive disorder[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding rapid cycling bipolar disorder is true?

options.text: Alcohol, stimulants, and caffeine use are risk factors.
It is defined as at least four episodes per month.
Hospitalization of these patients is rare.
It is more common in men than women.
It often responds to tricyclic antidepressants.

correct_answer.text: Alcohol, stimulants, and caffeine use are risk factors.

correct_answers.text: Alcohol, stimulants, and caffeine use are risk factors.

questions.explanation: Among the factors favoring the occurrence of rapid cycling bipolar disorder are alcohol, stimulant, and caffeine use[cite: 7]. Other factors include female gender because this subtype is much more common in women than men[cite: 7]. Most antidepressants readily induce excited episodes and thus aggravate the rapid cycling pattern[cite: 7]. Rapid cycling is defined as the occurrence of at least four episodes of depression and hypomania or mania per year (not per month)[cite: 7]. Hospitalization of these patients is often frequent to stabilize medication and achieve compliance[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: All of the following are common causes of misdiagnosis of mood disorder as schizophrenia except

options.text: reliance on the longitudinal rather than cross-sectional picture
flight of ideas perceived as loose associations
ascribing irritable mood to paranoid delusions
mistaking depressive depersonalization for schizophrenic emotional blunting
incomplete interepisodic recovery equated with schizophrenic defect

correct_answer.text: reliance on the longitudinal rather than cross-sectional picture

correct_answers.text: reliance on the longitudinal rather than cross-sectional picture

questions.explanation: Reliance on the cross-sectional rather than longitudinal picture (not vice versa) may cause a misdiagnosis of mood disorder as schizophrenia[cite: 7]. Cross-sectionally, young patients with bipolar disorder might seem psychotic and disorganized and thus schizophrenic[cite: 7]. Their thought processes are so rapid that they may seem loose, but unlike patients with schizophrenia, they display an expansive and elated affect, which is often contagious[cite: 7]. By contrast, a severely retarded bipolar depressive person, whose affect may superficially seem flat, almost never exhibits major fragmentation of thought[cite: 7]. The clinician should therefore place greater emphasis on the pattern of symptoms than on individual symptoms in the differential diagnosis of mood and schizophrenic psychosis[cite: 7]. Table 15.1 lists the most common pitfalls in diagnosis[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: All of the following statements regarding cyclothymic disorder are true except

options.text: Symptoms must be present for at least 2 years.
It occurs at the same rate in men and women.
Symptoms may satisfy criteria for major depression.
It consists of hypomania alternating with depressed mood.
Its lifetime prevalence rate is about 0.4 to 1 percent.

correct_answer.text: Symptoms may satisfy criteria for major depression.

correct_answers.text: Symptoms may satisfy criteria for major depression.

questions.explanation: Cyclothymia is characterized by at least 2 years of numerous periods with hypomanic symptoms and numerous periods with depressive symptoms that do not meet criteria for a major depressive episode[cite: 7]. This disorder apparently occurs at the same rate in both men and women, but women seek treatment more often than men[cite: 7]. The lifetime prevalence rate of cyclothymic disorder is 0.4 to 1 percent[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Dysthymic disorder differs from major depressive disorder because in dysthymic disorder,

options.text: the onset is usually late in life

correct_answer.text: the symptoms outnumber the signs

correct_answers.text: the symptoms outnumber the signs

questions.explanation: The profile of dysthymic disorder overlaps with that of major depressive disorder but differs from it in that symptoms tend to outnumber signs (more subjective than objective depression)[cite: 7]. This means that disturbances in appetite and libido are uncharacteristic, and psychomotor agitation or retardation is not observed[cite: 7]. This all translates into a depression with attenuated symptomatology[cite: 7]. Subtle endogenous features are observed, however, including inertia, lethargy, and anhedonia that are characteristically worse in the morning[cite: 7]. Dysthymic disorder is distinguished from major depressive disorder by the fact that patients complain that they have always been depressed[cite: 7]. Most cases are of early onset beginning in childhood or adolescence and certainly occurring by the time patients reach their 20s[cite: 7]. A late-onset subtype, which is much less prevalent and not well characterized clinically, has been identified among middle-aged and geriatric populations, largely through epidemiological studies in the community[cite: 7]. Diagnostic criteria stipulate the presence of depressed mood most of the time for at least 2 years (not episodic) or 1 year for children or adolescents[cite: 7]. Patients should not have symptoms that are better accounted for as major depressive disorder and should never have had a manic or hypomaniac episode[cite: 7]. The DSM-IV-TR allows clinicians to specify whether the onset was early (before age 21 years) or late (age 21 years or older)[cite: 7]. Dysthymic disorder refers to a subaffective or subclinical depressive disorder with (1) low-grade (not high-grade) chronicity for at least 2 years; (2) insidious onset, with the origin often in childhood or adolescence; and (3) a persistent or intermittent course[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Psychomotor retardation is characterized by all of the following except

correct_answer.text: restlessness

correct_answers.text: restlessness

questions.explanation: Features such as restlessness, agitation, and pressured speech are characteristic of psychomotor agitation, not retardation[cite: 7]. Psychomotor retardation, which is often present in depressed patients, manifests as paucity of spontaneous movements, reduced speech amplitude and flow, increased latency of responses, indecisiveness, poor concentration and forgetfulness, and overwhelming fatigue[cite: 7]. Brain imaging research that has revealed subcortical (extrapyramidal system) disturbances in mood disorders tends to support the centrality of psychomotor dysfunction in these disorders[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Features of anhedonia may include all of the following except

options.text: difficulty describing or being aware of emotions

correct_answer.text: difficulty describing or being aware of emotions

correct_answers.text: difficulty describing or being aware of emotions

questions.explanation: Anhedonia is one of the DSM IV-TR criteria for major depression[cite: 7]. Patients with severe depression and anhedonia may complain of being emotionally cut off from others and experience depersonalization in a world that seems strange to them (derealization)[cite: 7]. Loss of pleasure and withdrawal from previously enjoyable activities is typical of anhedonia[cite: 7]. The impact of the loss of emotional resonance can be so pervasive that patients may denounce values and beliefs that had previously given meaning to their lives (e.g., members of the clergy complain they no longer believe in the Church and have lost God)[cite: 7]. The inability of a person with depressive disorder to experience normal emotions (commonly observed among young depressed patients) differs from a schizophrenic person’s flat affect in that the loss of emotions is itself experienced as painful; that is, the patient suffers immensely from the inability to experience emotions[cite: 7]. Anhedonia does not typically include alexithymia, which is defined as a person’s inability to describe or be aware of one’s emotions or mood[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: The highest suicide rates are in which of the following age groups?

correct_answer.text: Older than age 65 years

correct_answers.text: Older than age 65 years

questions.explanation: Suicide is almost twice as frequent in older adults as in the general population[cite: 7]. The suicide rate for white men older than 65 years of age is five times higher than that of the general population[cite: 7]. Aging reduces suicide attempts but increases their lethality[cite: 7]. Depression is the most common psychiatric diagnosis in elderly suicide victims, unlike younger adults, in whom substance abuse alone or with comorbid mood disorders is the most frequent diagnosis[cite: 7]. Older patients with major medical illnesses or a recent loss should be evaluated for depressive symptomatology and suicidal ideation or plans, and aggressive treatment can help prevent their acting on suicidal thoughts[cite: 7]. Suicide rates are rising most rapidly in young adults, but the greatest risk remains in those people older than the age of 65 years[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best predictor of the likelihood of attempting suicide in the future?

correct_answer.text: Prior suicide attempt

correct_answers.text: Prior suicide attempt

questions.explanation: The strongest indicator of the likelihood of attempting suicide is a history of previous suicide attempts[cite: 7]. It has been shown that women make more suicidal gestures, but men are more likely to choose lethal methods and thus are more likely to successfully commit suicide[cite: 7]. Therefore, male gender is considered more a risk factor for suicide completion[cite: 7]. Alcohol or substance abuse, unemployment, and recent divorce are all additional risk factors but are less significant than a history of previous suicide attempts[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: In the differential diagnosis, the diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder should be restricted to

options.text: affective psychosis with concurrent brain disease
full affective and schizophrenic symptoms simultaneously
affective psychosis superimposed on mental retardation
a contagious expansive and elated affect

correct_answer.text: full affective and schizophrenic symptoms simultaneously

correct_answers.text: full affective and schizophrenic symptoms simultaneously

questions.explanation: The concept of schizoaffective (or cycloid) psychosis should be restricted to recurrent psychoses, with full affective and schizophrenic symptoms occurring nearly simultaneously during each episode[cite: 7]. This diagnosis should not be considered for a mood psychosis in which mood-incongruent psychotic features (e.g., Schneiderian and Bleulerian symptoms) can be explained on the basis of one of the following: (1) affective psychosis superimposed by mental retardation, giving rise to extremely hyperactive and bizarre manic behavior; (2) affective psychosis complicated by concurrent brain disease, substance abuse, or substantial withdrawal, known to give rise to numerous schneiderian symptoms; or (3) mixed episodes of bipolar disorder (which are notorious for signs and symptoms of psychotic disorganization)[cite: 7]. Official diagnostic systems use the category of schizoaffective disorder broadly[cite: 7]. Thus, patients with clear-cut manic episodes receive a schizoaffective diagnosis if delusions or hallucinations occur in the interepisodic period in the absence of prominent affective symptoms[cite: 7]. Many psychotic symptoms in mood disorders are often explanatory, whereby the patient tries to make sense of the core experiences of the affective illness[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Drugs that may precipitate mania include all of the following except

correct_answer.text: Propranolol

correct_answers.text: Propranolol

questions.explanation: Propranolol (Inderal), a β-blocker, is an antihypertensive and may actually cause depressive symptoms[cite: 7]. Many pharmacological agents, such as bromocriptine (Parlodel), isoniazid (Nydrazid), cimetidine (Tagamet), and disulfiram (Antabuse), may precipitate mania, as can antidepressant treatment or withdrawal[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants would not be the best choice for a patient with a history of suicidal ideation?

correct_answer.text: A tricyclic antidepressant

correct_answers.text: A tricyclic antidepressant

questions.explanation: In considering antidepressant use in suicidal or impulsive patients, caution should be taken in using medications that may be lethal in overdose (e.g., tricyclic antidepressants [TCA]) or that may exacerbate disinhibition or cognitive deficits (e.g., benzodiazepines)[cite: 7]. Therefore, it is not the best idea to prescribe a TCA to this patient[cite: 7]. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) are better choices[cite: 7]. Care should be taken to avoid precipitating a hypertensive crisis in patients taking MAOIs[cite: 7]. Bupropion and venlafaxine are other antidepressants that can be used alone or in combination with another medication[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is false?

options.text: ECT should be used in cases of psychotic depression only.
Bilateral ECT is somewhat more effective than unilateral ECT.
Retrograde memory impairment is a common side effect.
ECT is often used for refractory mood disorders.
Eight to 12 treatments are usually needed for symptomatic remission.

correct_answer.text: ECT should be used in cases of psychotic depression only.

correct_answers.text: ECT should be used in cases of psychotic depression only.

questions.explanation: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is effective in psychotic and nonpsychotic forms of depression[cite: 7]. Usually, 8 to 12 ECT treatments are required to achieve symptomatic remission, and this form of therapy has been shown to be effective even in patients who are refractory to several different medications[cite: 7]. Bilateral ECT is somewhat more effective than unilateral therapy, but bilateral ECT also appears to have more cognitive side effects, such as retrograde memory loss[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Mr. M is an 87-year-old man who, 6 weeks after a coronary artery bypass graft that was complicated by pneumonia and renal insufficiency, was admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation service for management of physical deconditioning. A psychiatrist was consulted 10 days after admission to rule out depression in the context of persistent low appetite and energy associated with suboptimal participation in rehabilitation. Mr. M reported no prior psychiatric history. He had worked as a chemist until retirement nearly 2 decades earlier. Laboratory examination revealed a low hematocrit of 21 and moderately elevated blood urea nitrogen of 65. On interview, Mr. M demonstrated psychomotor slowing and bland affect. He denied depression, hopelessness, worthlessness, and suicidal ideation. He expressed a desire to recover from his debilitated state but acknowledged uncertainty that he was capable of doing so. He also complained of extreme weakness. He stated, “I just don’t seem to have an appetite anymore.” Cognition largely was intact; there was mild short-term memory deficit. The most likely diagnosis in this patient is:

options.text: Mood disorder secondary to a general medical condition

correct_answer.text: Mood disorder secondary to a general medical condition

correct_answers.text: Mood disorder secondary to a general medical condition

questions.explanation: After an extended hospital course, many patients, like this one, demonstrate withdrawn behavior, anorexia, and fatigue, occasionally associated with mild cognitive loss, that do not meet criteria for cognitive or mood disorder but are a direct product of resolving medical illness and associated debilitation[cite: 7]. The likelihood that a mood disorder is due to a general medical condition is increased if a temporal relationship exists between the onset, exacerbation, or remission of the medical condition and the mood disorder[cite: 7]. Atypical features (e.g., unusual age of onset, lack of family history, and lack of prior episodes of mood disorder) also raise the likelihood of a medical basis for mood symptoms[cite: 7]. Mild short-term memory deficits can be normal with aging and do not necessarily indicate that Mr. M has dementia[cite: 7]. He also demonstrated largely intact cognition, making delirium an unlikely diagnosis[cite: 7]. Patients with a diagnosis of anxiety disorder with depressed mood primarily exhibit symptoms of anxiety states, such as marked tension, phobias, and panic attacks, all of which predate any depressive symptoms[cite: 7]. In addition, anxiety disorders rarely appear for the first time after 40 years of age[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: A 19-year-old single woman presented with the chief complaint that “all men are bastards.” Since her early teens, with the onset of her menses, she had complained of extreme variability in her moods on a nearly daily basis; irritability with hostile outbursts was her main affect, although more protracted hypersomnic depressions with multiple overdoses and wrist slashings had led to at least three hospitalizations. She also had migrainous headaches that, according to her mother, had motivated at least one of those overdoses. Despite her tempestuous and suicidal moods that led to these hospitalizations, she complained of “inner emptiness and a bottomless void.” She had used heroin, alcohol, and stimulants to overcome this troubling symptom. She said that she was mentally disturbed because of a series of stepfathers who had all forced “oral rape” on her when she was between 11 and 15 years of age. She subsequently became sexually involved with any man that she met in bars, no longer knowing whether she was a “prostitute” or a “nice little girl.” On two occasions, she had inflicted cigarette burns inside her vagina “to feel something.” She had also engaged in a “brief lesbian relationship” that ultimately left her “emptier” and guilt ridden; nonetheless, she now believed that she should burn in hell because she could not get rid of “obsessing” about the excitement of mutual cunnilingus with her much older female partner. The patient was given phenelzine (Nardil), eventually increased to 75 mg per day, at which point the mother described her as “the sweet daughter she was before age 13.” At her next premenstrual phase, the patient developed insomnia, ran away from home at night, started “dancing like a go-go girl, met an incredibly handsome man” of 45 years of age (a pornography shop owner), and had a clandestine marriage to him. Other than a mood disorder, this patient also shows signs of

correct_answer.text: borderline personality disorder

correct_answers.text: borderline personality disorder

questions.explanation: This case illustrates the intimate relationship among atypical depression, borderline personality disorder, and bipolar II disorder[cite: 7]. These three conditions, listed as distinct nosological entities in the DSM-IV-TR, may nonetheless share an underlying psychobiological or genetic diathesis[cite: 7]. The complaint is often heard that even when a mood disorder is diagnosed in a “borderline” patient, response to antidepressants is disappointing[cite: 7]. The problem is that affective disorders in these patients usually conform to bipolar II disorder—often complicated by ultrarapid cycling—and many clinicians trained in an earlier era, including some with a biological orientation, may lack sufficient experience in the art of pharmacologically managing patients who markedly deviate from classic bipolar I disorder[cite: 7]. Recently, lamotrigine has shown promise for such patients[cite: 7]. Table 15.2 shows that the overlap between borderline personality and mood disorders is extensive, so giving a borderline diagnosis to a person with mood disorder is redundant[cite: 7]. Use of personality disorder diagnoses may lead to a neglect of the mood disorder or, perhaps, half-hearted treatment of the mood disorder; failure to respond would then be blamed on the patient’s “self-defeating character” or “resistance to getting well,” thus exculpating the clinician[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with major depressive disorder. For the past 8 months, she has had a depressed mood, decreased energy and concentration, and loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities. Although she never attempted suicide, she acknowledges that she thought she would probably jump off a local bridge if she ever had the chance. She denies any history of excessively elevated moods. You decide to start her on antidepressant therapy. Two weeks later, this patient is at greatest risk for

correct_answer.text: suicide completion

correct_answers.text: suicide completion

questions.explanation: When antidepressant medications first begin to work, patients tend to report an increase in energy levels before significant improvement in mood symptoms[cite: 7]. For this reason, carrying out suicide plansis more of a risk during this period[cite: 7]. Medication noncompliance with effective psychopharmacological treatments during both acute and maintenance therapy is a major cause of morbidity among patients with schizophrenia and disorders with poor insight, not among patients with depression[cite: 7]. Although noncompliance is a possibility with any patient, it is not the best choice listed[cite: 7]. This patient has nothing in her history to indicate bipolar disorder as a more appropriate diagnosis; therefore, there is no reason to believe manic or hypomanic episodes will be precipitated by antidepressant use[cite: 7]. Extrapyramidal symptoms are a consequence of typical antipsychotic use, not antidepressant use[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: A 57-year-old woman presents to you after being diagnosed with major depressive disorder. She has been depressed ever since the death of her husband 2 years earlier. She has been taking the same antidepressant since her diagnosis 1 year ago, with no relief of her symptoms. She states that she would like your help in ending her life. The best option for your next step is:

options.text: respect the patient’s wishes because she is of sound mind
seek to more adequately treat her depression
seek family members to make a more informed decision
obtain information from the state regarding physician-assisted suicide laws

correct_answer.text: seek to more adequately treat her depression

correct_answers.text: seek to more adequately treat her depression

questions.explanation: Much political and theological heat has been generated in recent years by the debate on physician-assisted suicide[cite: 7]. Many of the patients requesting death are depressed and would be likely to respond to psychotherapy, pharmacotherapy, or both[cite: 7]. Frequently, they have been inadequately diagnosed or treated[cite: 7]. Active depression can be considered a state of incompetence, making such patients unable to make informed decisions for themselves[cite: 7]. Family members or a living will should be consulted only in cases of medical emergencies in which decisions must be made immediately[cite: 7]. In this case, treating the patient’s depression is the best option[cite: 7]. It is not necessary to involve the hospital ethics committee in this decision[cite: 7]. Currently, Oregon is the only state that has passed enabling laws regarding physician-assisted suicide[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Ms. S, a 24-year-old woman, is brought for a psychiatric consultation by her mother who complains of bizarre behavior. One month ago, Ms. S was fired from her job at a local bookstore because of frequently arriving late and not performing her duties adequately. She states that she fell in love with another employee and tried to get his attention and spend time with him even though he seemed uninterested. Over the past 3 months, she increased her use of alcohol and marijuana to three beers and two to three joints per day. Her mother reports a 2-week history of increased energy, eating little, talking a great deal, and interrupting others frequently. A week ago, Ms. S reported that her former work colleagues were plotting against her and attempting to control her by broadcasting thoughts into her brain. She did not sleep the previous 2 nights. Ms. S has no significant psychiatric or medical history. She takes no medications. Physical examination reveals a blood pressure of 135/75 mm Hg, heart rate of 84 beats/min, and temperature of 37◦C. Her conjunctivae are pink, and her pupils are equal, 3 mm, and reactive to light. Deep tendon reflexes are normal throughout. Urine toxicology reveals the presence of cannabinoids. On mental status testing, her mood is euphoric, her speech is pressured, and she is emotionally labile and irritable. Her thinking is illogical and disorganized. She denies hallucinations. She is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Immediate recall and recent and remote memory are intact. Throughout the interview, she is preoccupied by thoughts of the coworker with whom she has fallen in love. Ms. S is admitted to a psychiatric unit, and treatment is initiated with haloperidol, 10 mg/day, which is increased to 20 mg/day on day 5 because of continued agitation. On day 6, she becomes withdrawn and uncommunicative. She is diffusely rigid with a temperature of 39◦C. Her white blood count is 14,300 and her creatinine phosphokinase is 2,100. Several blood cultures are negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis at the time of admission?

correct_answer.text: Bipolar disorder

correct_answers.text: Bipolar disorder

questions.explanation: The diagnosis of bipolar disorder best fits the history and symptoms, but it is by no means certain[cite: 7]. She presents with a 1-month history of impaired judgment and erratic behavior followed by increased energy, pressured speech, mood lability, and decreased need for sleep, all of which indicate a manic episode[cite: 7]. The emergence of paranoid delusions is also consistent with mania, and a single manic episode, with or without major depressive episodes, qualifies for a diagnosis of bipolar disorder[cite: 7]. That diagnosis can only be made, however, if it is believed that the symptoms are not the result of a general medical condition or substance use[cite: 7]. We know that she has been using increased amounts of marijuana and alcohol and that she is probably intoxicated with marijuana at the time of admission[cite: 7]. Heavy marijuana use in some individuals can cause a psychotic state with paranoid delusions and hallucinations[cite: 7]. There are some features, however, that are inconsistent with a purely marijuana-induced state, which more typically presents with decreased talkativeness and long response latency than with the pressured speech seen here[cite: 7]. In addition, increased energy and activity and decreased need for sleep are much more likely in bipolar disorder than in a marijuana psychosis[cite: 7]. The delusional belief of her thoughts being controlled by an outside force is strikingly similar to delusions of control that are so often seen in schizophrenia, but the prominent mood symptoms and time course (1 month) preclude that diagnosis[cite: 7]. The diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder would require a 2-week period of psychotic symptoms without prominent mood symptoms, which is not the case here[cite: 7]. An erotomanic delusional belief is that the patient is loved by another (often famous) person, not as is the case here, which the patient herself is preoccupied with being in love with someone else[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her behavior on day 6?

correct_answer.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

correct_answers.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

questions.explanation: The events of days 5 and 6 almost certainly represent the emergence of a neuroleptic malignant syndrome, an idiosyncratic response to antipsychotics (especially high-potency, typical agents) characterized by fever, rigidity, and obtundation[cite: 7]. The clinical diagnosis is confirmed, with the typical findings of leukocytosis and greatly increased creatinine phosphokinase (CPK)[cite: 7]. Anticholinergic delirium includes fever but not the rigidity or laboratory findings[cite: 7]. In addition, patients with an anticholinergic delirium are more likely to be agitated than withdrawn[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: Which of the following pharmacologic approaches is most appropriate on day 6?

options.text: Stop haloperidol, add bromocriptine, and seek medical consultation.
Continue the same dose of haloperidol and add risperidone.
Continue the same dose of haloperidol and add benztropine.

correct_answer.text: Stop haloperidol, add bromocriptine, and seek medical consultation.

correct_answers.text: Stop haloperidol, add bromocriptine, and seek medical consultation.

questions.explanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a life-threatening medical emergency[cite: 7]. All medications must be stopped; switching to an atypical agent such as risperidone will not help her[cite: 7]. Appropriate treatment includes life support, maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance, and decreasing her fever[cite: 7]. Bromocriptine is a centrally acting dopamine agonist that presumably works by reversing the effects of the antipsychotic-caused dopamine blockade[cite: 7]. The treatment of NMS commonly combines bromocriptine with dantrolene, a peripheral muscle relaxant[cite: 7]. Consultation with the medical service is crucial because the treatment may be complex[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: A suicidal patient with chronic depressive disorder presents to your office very frustrated and in tears. He tells you he cannot stop thinking about ending his life because he is so depressed. You ask him if he has a plan, and he details where he could buy a handgun and where he would go to shoot himself. You fear the patient will carry out this plan because he has not had adequate control of his symptoms since his last antidepressant change 1 month ago. You discuss inpatient hospitalization for medication stabilization, but the patient refuses. You’re next step in management of this patient would best be:

options.text: Admit the patient to the hospital anyway.
Give the latest antidepressant more time to take affect.
Change to another class of antidepressant.
Try to persuade the patient to admit himself to the hospital.
Initiate psychotherapy to discuss the reasons behind the suicidal thoughts.

correct_answer.text: Admit the patient to the hospital anyway.

correct_answers.text: Admit the patient to the hospital anyway.

questions.explanation: Suicidal patients with intent and specific plans should always be taken seriously[cite: 7]. For patients believed to be too much at risk for outpatient therapy or partial hospital programs, inpatient treatment is required[cite: 7]. Such hospitalization is preferably on a voluntary basis, but if the patient refuses, involuntary admission is required[cite: 7]. The options of changing antidepressants and giving more time for the medication to take effect are not the best options in this circumstance, although they may be in patients when suicide is less of an acute risk[cite: 7]. Psychotherapy is also not an option when immediate intervention is needed with actively suicidal patients[cite: 7]. Contact with the family and friends of suicidal patients is essential, and maintaining patient confidentiality is not mandatory if divulged material is believed to be necessary to protect the patient’s life[cite: 7]. Some patients appear so imminently and acutely suicidal that the clinician is afraid to let them out of the office[cite: 7]. Patients can be admitted to the hospital against their will if they are a danger to themselves or to other people[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: A 64-year-old woman with an extensive smoking history has recently been diagnosed with small cell lung cancer. She develops a depressed mood, decreased interests, and difficulty concentrating soon thereafter because she reports she cannot stop thinking about how worthless her life has been. She eats incessantly and has gained 10 lb in the last 5 weeks; she also reports increased sleep. You decide to prescribe phenelzine for her symptoms of atypical depression. Which of the following is contraindicated in those patients taking phenelzine?

correct_answer.text: Fluoxetine

correct_answers.text: Fluoxetine

questions.explanation: MAOIs have been shown to be particularly effective in the treatment of patients with atypical depression[cite: 7]. Important side effects of MAOI therapy include hypertensive crisis and serotonin syndrome[cite: 7]. Hypertensive crisis can be precipitated when foods rich in tyramine (e.g., wine, cheese) are ingested by someone who is taking an MAOI[cite: 7]. Serotonin syndrome is caused by the interaction of an MAOI with a SSRI, pseudoephedrine, or meperidine[cite: 7]. Serotonin syndrome is characterized by hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, and altered mental status[cite: 7]. Therefore, fluoxetine, an SSRI, is contraindicated in this patient[cite: 7].

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman presents to a clinic with a chief complaint of fatigue. She states that this feeling of “being tired” has persisted for the past 4 years. She has lost 12 lb over the past 2 years and admits to overeating. The patient states that she sleeps at least 11 hours per night. She denies suicidal ideation but complains about not being able to concentrate. What is the likely diagnosis?

correct_answer.text: Dysthymia

correct_answers.text: Dysthymia

questions.explanation: Given the chronological course and degree of severity of the patient’s symptoms, the most likely diagnosis is dysthymia[cite: 7]. Dysthymia is diagnosed when a patient experiences depressed mood for most of the day for a minimum of 2 years plus at least two of the following: insomnia or hypersomnia, poor concentration, low energy, change in appetite, or lack of self-worth[cite: 7]. Unlike dysthymia, in major depressive disorder, patients must have five or more symptoms for most of the day over 2 weeks[cite: 7]. Generalized anxiety disorder is characterized by sleep disturbance, irritability, inability to concentrate, uncontrollable worrying, and fatigue[cite: 7]. Substance abuse is a possible, although it is a less likely diagnosis given the duration of symptoms[cite: 7].

questions.explanation: Bereaved persons exhibit many depressive symptoms during the first 1 to 2 years after their loss[cite: 7]. However, there is a distinction between depression and bereavement[cite: 7]. Whereas grieving persons and their relatives perceive bereavement as a normal reaction to the loss, those with depressive disorder often view themselves as sick and may actually believe they are losing their minds[cite: 7]. Active suicidal ideation is rare in grief but common in major depressive disorder[cite: 7]. questions.explanation: Tricyclic antidepressants such as imipramine (Tofranil) are known for their cardiotoxicity because they prolong cardiac conduction time and can cause a variety of arrhythmias[cite: 7]. Also among the substantial side effects of tricyclic antidepressants are weight gain, sedation, anticholinergic effects, and orthostatic hypotension[cite: 7]. Weight gain is also a common adverse effect of clozapine (Clozaril), as well as agranulocytosis; therefore, weekly blood monitoring is necessary[cite: 7]. Neither clozapine nor imipramine acts as norepinephrine partial agonists; instead, clozapine acts by blockade of serotonin-2a and D2 receptors, and imipramine acts by reducing the reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin[cite: 7]. There are no known teratogenic effects of clozapine or imipramine[cite: 7].

It is a condition characterized by vague functional physical and mental fatigue[cite: 7]. The anxiety generated by overstimulation is so excessive that it is replaced by a chronic disposition to irritability, fatigue (especially mental fatigue), lethargy, and exhaustion[cite: 7]. It seems as if the patient’s mind refuses to take on new stresses[cite: 7]. Anxious manifestations include headache, backache, heavy limbs, vague neuralgias, yawning, dyspepsia, palpitations, sweating of the hands and feet, chills, flushing, sensitivity to weather changes, insomnia, nightmares, pantophobia, asthenopia, and tinnitus[cite: 7]. Cyclothymic disorder is characterized by frequent short cycles of subsyndromal mild depression and hypomania[cite: 7]. The course of cyclothymia is continuous or intermittent, with infrequent periods of euthymia[cite: 7]. Shifts in mood often lack adequate precipitants[cite: 7]. Persons with cyclothymic disorder are dilettantes; they show great promise in many areas but rarely bring any of their efforts to fruition[cite: 7]. Hypomania occurring as part of bipolar II disorder rarely progresses to manic psychosis, and insight is relatively preserved[cite: 7]. Hypomania refers to a distinct period of at least a few days of mild elevation of mood, sharpened and positive thinking, and increased energy and activity levels, typically without the impairment characteristic of manic episodes[cite: 7]. It is not merely a milder form of mania[cite: 7]. Hypomania is distinguished from mere happiness in that it tends to recur and can sometimes be mobilized by antidepressants[cite: 7]. The most typical developmental background of dysthymic disorder is an insidious onset of depression dating back to late childhood or the teens, preceding any superimposed major depressive episodes by years or even decades[cite: 7]. The typical features of dysthymic disorder are the presence of a depressed mood that lasts most of the day and is present almost continuously[cite: 7]. There are associated feeling of inadequacy, guilt, irritability, and anger; withdrawal from society; loss of interest; and inactivity and lack of productivity[cite: 7]. It differs from major depression in that patients complain that they have always been depressed[cite: 7]. The designation bipolar I disorder is synonymous with what was formally known as bipolar disorder—a syndrome in which a complete set of mania symptoms occurs during the course of the disorder[cite: 7]. Typically beginning in the teenage years, the 20s, or the 30s, the first episode could be manic, depressive, or mixed[cite: 7]. Bipolar I disorder, single manic episode, describes patients having a first episode of mania (most such patients eventually develop depressive episodes)[cite: 7]. Bipolar I disorder, recurrent, is diagnosed on the basis of the symptoms of the most recent episode (i.e., bipolar I disorder, most recent episode manic; bipolar disorder I disorder, most recent episode depressed)[cite: 7]. Bipolar II disorder is characterized by depressive episodes and hypomanic episodes, but the episodes of manic-like symptoms do not quite meet the diagnostic criteria for a full manic syndrome[cite: 7]. A few studies indicate that bipolar II disorder is associated with more marital disruption and with an onset at an earlier age than bipolar I disorder[cite: 7]. Evidence also indicates that patients with bipolar II disorder are at greater risk of both attempting and completing suicide than patients with bipolar I disorder or major depressive disorder[cite: 7].
